title: Characterization of ALD-Grown Al2O3 Thin Films Transferred from Sacrificial Polymer Substrates
content: Atomic layer deposition (ALD) is widely used to grow gate dielectrics directly onto semiconductor materials in conventional field effect transistors (FETs). However, as device scaling pushes beyond silicon—aiming for gate lengths below 10 nm and channel thicknesses below 2 nm—2D material device integration is essential [1, 2, 3]. 2D semiconductors pose a significant challenge for ALD due to their inert surfaces, which lack the dangling bonds necessary for effective film growth [4]. Here we characterize aluminum oxide (Al2O3) thin films grown on sacrificial poly vinyl alcohol substrates by ALD. These films are transferred to target surfaces via van der Waals stacking. High-quality FETs fabricated by this technique were previously reported elsewhere [5], but the compositional, structural, and morphological qualities of these films is not well understood. These properties are critical to understanding how the sacrificial layer growth and transfer process may introduce defects, strain, wrinkles, or contamination.
